claim: Wounding the C. elegans epidermis with a 405 nm laser triggers an immune reaction and a repair response.
source: In Caenorhabditis elegans, wounding the epidermis triggers an immune reaction and a repair response, but it is not clear how these are coordinated.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact from prior work.

claim: The microtubule cytoskeleton is implicated in the maintenance of epidermal integrity.
source: Previous work implicated the microtubule cytoskeleton in the maintenance of epidermal integrity (Chuang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chuang et al., 2016.

claim: Wounding provokes a reorganisation of plasma membrane subdomains.
source: Here, by establishing a simple wounding system, we show that wounding provokes a reorganisation of plasma membrane subdomains.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The microtubule plus end-binding protein EB1/EBP-2 is recruited around the wound following membrane reorganization.
source: This is followed by recruitment of the microtubule plus end-binding protein EB1/EBP-2 around the wound and actin ring formation, dependent on ARP2/3 branched actin polymerisation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental observations in the manuscript.

claim: Actin ring formation following wounding is dependent on ARP2/3 branched actin polymerisation.
source: This is followed by recruitment of the microtubule plus end-binding protein EB1/EBP-2 around the wound and actin ring formation, dependent on ARP2/3 branched actin polymerisation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Microtubule dynamics are required for the recruitment and closure of the actin ring.
source: We show that microtubule dynamics are required for the recruitment and closure of the actin ring, and for the trafficking of the key signalling protein SLC6/SNF-12 toward the injury site.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Microtubule dynamics are required for the trafficking of the key signalling protein SLC6/SNF-12 toward the injury site.
source: We show that microtubule dynamics are required for the recruitment and closure of the actin ring, and for the trafficking of the key signalling protein SLC6/SNF-12 toward the injury site.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Without SNF-12 recruitment, there is an abrogation of the immune response.
source: Without SNF-12 recruitment, there is an abrogation of the immune response.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Microtubule dynamics coordinate the cytoskeletal changes required for wound repair and the concomitant activation of innate immunity.
source: Our results suggest that microtubule dynamics coordinate the cytoskeletal changes required for wound repair and the concomitant activation of innate immunity.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, based on the experimental findings presented.

claim: The fungus Drechmeria coniospora infects C. elegans by piercing the cuticle and growing through the underlying epidermis.
source: In one well-studied example, when the fungus Drechmeria coniospora infects Caenorhabditis elegans, by piercing the cuticle and growing through the underlying epidermis, it triggers an innate immune response, characterized by the induction of expression of a battery of antimicrobial peptide (AMP) genes (Pujol et al., 2008b; Taffoni and Pujol, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pujol et al., 2008b and Taffoni and Pujol, 2015.

claim: Drechmeria coniospora infection triggers an innate immune response characterized by the induction of expression of antimicrobial peptide (AMP) genes.
source: In one well-studied example, when the fungus Drechmeria coniospora infects Caenorhabditis elegans, by piercing the cuticle and growing through the underlying epidermis, it triggers an innate immune response, characterized by the induction of expression of a battery of antimicrobial peptide (AMP) genes (Pujol et al., 2008b; Taffoni and Pujol, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pujol et al., 2008b and Taffoni and Pujol, 2015.

claim: The nlp-29 cluster genes are principally controlled in a cell autonomous manner.
source: These include the genes of the nlp-29 cluster (Pujol et al., 2012), which are principally controlled in a cell autonomous manner (Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pujol et al., 2012 and Lee et al., 2018.

claim: Sterile wounding upregulates the expression of the nlp-29 cluster.
source: Sterile wounding also upregulates the expression of the nlp-29 cluster (Pujol et al., 2008a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pujol et al., 2008a.

claim: Changes in gene expression upon infection and wounding result from the activation of the GPCR DCAR-1 that acts upstream of a conserved p38 MAPK signalling cassette.
source: In both cases, these changes in gene expression result from the activation of the GPCR DCAR-1 that acts upstream of a conserved p38 MAPK signalling cassette (Zugasti et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zugasti et al., 2014.

claim: The p38 MAPK PMK-1 acts upstream of the STAT transcription factor-like protein STA-2.
source: The p38 MAPK PMK-1 itself acts upstream of the STAT transcription factor-like protein STA-2.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Activation of STA-2 is believed to require the SLC6 family protein SNF-12.
source: Although the precise details are as yet unclear, activation of STA-2 is believed to require the SLC6 family protein SNF-12 (Dierking et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dierking et al., 2011.

claim: Triggering the immune response upon wounding has a prophylactic role and is a safeguard against the potential entry of pathogenic microbes.
source: Triggering the immune response upon wounding has a prophylactic role and is a safeguard against the potential entry of pathogenic microbes.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the biological function.

claim: Skin wounding in C. elegans triggers a Ca2+-dependent signalling cascade that promotes wound repair through actin ring closure.
source: Thus, in addition to AMP gene induction, skin wounding in C. elegans also triggers a Ca2+-dependent signalling cascade that promotes wound repair through actin ring closure (Xu and Chisholm, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Xu and Chisholm, 2011.

claim: The nematode skin is mainly a syncytium, with a single multinucleate epidermal cell, hyp7, covering the whole animal except at the head and tail.
source: The nematode skin is mainly a syncytium. Except at the head and tail, a single multinucleate epidermal cell, hyp7, covers the whole animal (Altun and Hall, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Altun and Hall, 2014.

claim: Repair processes in C. elegans epidermis exhibit some characteristics previously described for single cell wound repair in other organisms.
source: Its repair processes exhibit some of the characteristics previously described for single cell wound repair in other organisms (Sonnemann and Bement, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sonnemann and Bement, 2011.

claim: Actin ring closure in C. elegans does not rely on myosin-II contractility and the 'purse string' mechanism described in other organisms.
source: On the other hand, actin ring closure in C. elegans does not rely on myosin-II contractility and the 'purse string' mechanism described in other organisms (Begnaud et al., 2016), but instead requires Arp2/3-dependent actin polymerization (Xu and Chisholm, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Begnaud et al., 2016 and Xu and Chisholm, 2011.

claim: Actin ring closure in C. elegans requires Arp2/3-dependent actin polymerization.
source: On the other hand, actin ring closure in C. elegans does not rely on myosin-II contractility and the 'purse string' mechanism described in other organisms (Begnaud et al., 2016), but instead requires Arp2/3-dependent actin polymerization (Xu and Chisholm, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Xu and Chisholm, 2011.

claim: In Xenopus laevis oocytes, microtubules were shown to be required to restrict the assembly zone of actin and myosin around the wound edge.
source: In a single-cell wound-healing model using Xenopus laevis oocytes, MTs were shown to be required to restrict the assembly zone of actin and myosin around the wound edge (Bement et al., 1999; Mandato and Bement, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bement et al., 1999 and Mandato and Bement, 2003.

claim: Perturbation of MT dynamics in a D. melanogaster EB1 mutant resulted in a delay of actomyosin assembly at the wound edge in multi-cellular wounds.
source: A study in D. melanogaster embryos also revealed that perturbation of MT dynamics, in a + end-binding protein 1 (EB1) mutant, resulted in a delay of actomyosin assembly at the wound edge in multi-cellular wounds (Abreu-Blanco et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Abreu-Blanco et al., 2012.

claim: The direct role of MTs in the C. elegans wound response has not been previously addressed.
source: The direct role of MTs in the C. elegans wound response has not been previously addressed.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the literature.

claim: Loss of DAPK-1 causes both undue tissue repair and an inappropriate activation of an immune response.
source: Earlier work had shown that loss of DAPK-1, homolog of death-associated protein kinase, causes both undue tissue repair and an inappropriate activation of an immune response (Tong et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tong et al., 2009.

claim: Loss of dapk-1 function causes excessive MT stabilization.
source: A more recent study showed that loss of dapk-1 function causes excessive MT stabilization (Chuang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chuang et al., 2016.

claim: MT stability could directly influence immune signalling.
source: These results suggest that MT stability could directly influence immune signalling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited studies.

claim: The adult epidermis in C. elegans is a single cell layer, covered on its apical surface by an impermeable cuticle that serves as an exoskeleton.
source: The adult epidermis in C. elegans is a single cell layer, covered on its apical surface by an impermeable cuticle that serves as an exoskeleton.
evidence: This is stated as established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The epidermal syncytium hyp7 can be divided into two distinct regions: one lateral where the nuclei and most of the cytoplasm are, and the dorso-ventral part above the muscles.
source: The epidermal syncytium hyp7 can be divided into two distinct regions, one lateral, where the nuclei and most of the cytoplasm are, and the dorso-ventral part above the muscles where the apical and basolateral plasma membranes of hyp7 are juxtaposed and crossed by hemidesmosomes that anchor the muscles to the cuticle exoskeleton (Figure 1A; Altun and Hall, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Altun and Hall, 2014 and Figure 1A.

claim: The plasma membrane can be perforated in an extremely targeted manner using standard 405 nm microscopy imaging lasers.
source: Previous studies on Xenopus oocytes have demonstrated that the plasma membrane can be perforated in an extremely targeted manner using standard 405 nm microscopy imaging lasers (Burkel et al., 2012; Mandato and Bement, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Burkel et al., 2012 and Mandato and Bement, 2001.

claim: The hyp7 lateral syncytial epidermis of C. elegans can be efficiently wounded with a short pulse of 405 nm laser light.
source: We found that we could efficiently wound the hyp7 lateral syncytial epidermis of C. elegans (Figure 1A) with a short pulse of 405 nm laser light (maximum power for 1–3 s) in Fluorescence Recovery After Photobleaching (FRAP) mode.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data and Figure 1A.

claim: Wounding with a 405 nm laser causes an immediate autofluorescent scar.
source: Using this system, we first confirmed all the previously described wound hallmarks (Pujol et al., 2008a; Xu and Chisholm, 2011), such as an immediate autofluorescent scar, a Ca2+ burst, the formation of an actin ring and later the induction of AMP reporter gene expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by citations and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Wounding with a 405 nm laser causes a Ca2+ burst.
source: Using this system, we first confirmed all the previously described wound hallmarks (Pujol et al., 2008a; Xu and Chisholm, 2011), such as an immediate autofluorescent scar, a Ca2+ burst, the formation of an actin ring and later the induction of AMP reporter gene expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by citations and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Wounding with a 405 nm laser causes the formation of an actin ring.
source: Using this system, we first confirmed all the previously described wound hallmarks (Pujol et al., 2008a; Xu and Chisholm, 2011), such as an immediate autofluorescent scar, a Ca2+ burst, the formation of an actin ring and later the induction of AMP reporter gene expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by citations and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Wounding with a 405 nm laser causes later induction of AMP reporter gene expression.
source: Using this system, we first confirmed all the previously described wound hallmarks (Pujol et al., 2008a; Xu and Chisholm, 2011), such as an immediate autofluorescent scar, a Ca2+ burst, the formation of an actin ring and later the induction of AMP reporter gene expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by citations and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: In Xenopus oocytes, a wound is rapidly patched through mobilisation and recruitment of membrane from a local pool of vesicles.
source: In Xenopus oocytes, a wound is rapidly patched through mobilisation and recruitment of membrane from a local pool of vesicles (Davenport et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Davenport et al., 2016.

claim: Within 15 s after wounding, large heterogeneous membrane domains that are normally stable regrouped and extended towards the wound.
source: Within 15 s after wounding, large heterogeneous membrane domains that are normally stable regrouped and extended towards the wound (Figure 1C, Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and Figure 1C.

claim: PIP2 has been found segregated into distinct membrane pools in the plasma membrane in other species.
source: PIP2 has been found segregated into distinct membrane pools in the plasma membrane in other species, consistent with its wide range of cellular functions including regulating the adhesion between the actin-based cortical cytoskeleton and the plasma membrane (Raucher et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Raucher et al., 2000.

claim: The plasma membrane of the hyp7 syncytium is heterogeneously labelled with PIP2.
source: We found that the plasma membrane of the hyp7 syncytium was also heterogeneously labelled using a strain in which PIP2 was specifically labelled (wrt-2p::GFP::PH-PLC1δ Wildwater et al., 2011); these membrane domains were relatively static.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and citation to Wildwater et al., 2011.

claim: Upon wounding, there is a rapid but transient disappearance of the PIP2 signal in a larger area than the wound.
source: Upon wounding, we observed a rapid but transient disappearance of the signal in a larger area than the wound.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental observations.

claim: There is a reorganization of PIP2 membrane domains around the wound after 15 to 30 s, followed by appearance of cytoplasmic vesicles below the plasma membrane.
source: There was then a reorganization of these membrane domains around the wound after 15 to 30 s, followed by appearance of cytoplasmic vesicles below the plasma membrane (Figure 1D, Figure 1—video 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and Figure 1D.

claim: These processes are likely to provide an immediate barrier preventing the potential leakage of cellular components, followed by a restoration of membrane integrity.
source: These processes are likely to provide an immediate barrier preventing the potential leakage of cellular components, followed by a restoration of membrane integrity as previously proposed in other systems (Davenport et al., 2016; Nakamura et al., 2018; Vaughan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations and supported by citations.

claim: Under resting condition in the young adult, in the lateral epidermis, actin is observed in a disorganised pattern of foci linked with fine filaments.
source: Under resting condition in the young adult, in the lateral epidermis, we observed a disorganised pattern of foci linked with fine filaments (Figure 2A, bw (before wound)).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and Figure 2A.

claim: Upon wounding, actin was recruited as a wave to the wound site within 2–4 min and formed a well-defined actin ring after 5 min.
source: Upon wounding, while the pre-existing actin filaments appeared stable, actin was recruited as a wave to the wound site within 2–4 min and formed a well-defined actin ring after 5 min (n > 100).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: The actin ring subsequently constricted as the wound closed.
source: This ring subsequently constricted as the wound closed (Figure 2A and Figure 2—video 1), in line with previous observations (Xu and Chisholm, 2011).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data, Figure 2A, and citation to Xu and Chisholm, 2011.

claim: Laser wounding causes ARP2/ARX-2 recruitment at the wound site.
source: Laser wounding also causes ARP2/ARX-2 and EB1 recruitment at the wound site as visualized in strains ARX-2::GFP KI (B) and col-19p::EBP-2::GFP (C), respectively.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and Figure 2B.

claim: ARX-2/ARP2 was recruited to the wound with a pattern similar to actin.
source: We could observe a recruitment of ARX-2/ARP2 to the wound with a pattern similar to actin (Figure 2B, Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and Figure 2B.

claim: The actin ring closes due to polymerisation of branched actin network.
source: These results reinforce the hypothesis that the actin ring closes due to polymerisation of branched actin network.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations of ARX-2/ARP2 recruitment.

claim: EB1::GFP exhibited rapid, comet-like movement throughout hyp7 under resting conditions, with a speed of 0.26 ± 0.10 µm/s.
source: Under resting conditions EB1::GFP exhibited rapid, comet-like movement throughout hyp7, with a speed (0.26 ± 0.10 µm/s, Figure 2—source data 1) similar to the speed previously determined (0.3 µm/s) (Chuang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and citation to Chuang et al., 2016.

claim: Upon wounding, EB1::GFP comets accumulated within 2 min around the wound site.
source: Upon wounding, EB1::GFP comets accumulated within 2 min around the wound site (n > 50, Figure 2C and Figure 2—video 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and Figure 2C.

claim: Upon wounding, there was a small reduction of EB1 comet average speed in the vicinity of the wound, to 0.16 ± 0.06 µm/s.
source: This was concomitant with a small reduction of their average speed in the vicinity of the wound, to 0.16 ± 0.06 µm/s (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: When actin and EB1 were visualised simultaneously, EB1 was found associated with the actin ring as it closes, with a preferential localisation at the leading edge.
source: When actin and EB1 were visualised simultaneously, EB1 was found associated with the actin ring as it closes, with a preferential localisation at the leading edge (Figure 2D, Figure 2—videos 4 and 5).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and Figure 2D.

claim: DNC-2 was recruited at the inner edge of the actin ring.
source: Using a dynactin reporter previously shown to be associated with MT + tips in C. elegans, DNC-2::GFP (Barbosa et al., 2017), we observed that there was a similar recruitment of DNC-2 at the inner edge of the actin ring (Figure 2E, Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data, Figure 2E, and citation to Barbosa et al., 2017.

claim: Kymograph analyses of the EB1 signal revealed two phases, the first one almost 10 times more rapid than the subsequent one.
source: Kymograph analyses of the EB1 signal revealed two phases, the first one almost 10 times more rapid that the subsequent one (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and Figure 2F.

claim: The speed of EB1 ring closure (0.008 µm/s) was almost 2 orders of magnitude slower than the speed of the EB1 comets (0.26 µm/s).
source: Notably, the speed of EB1 ring closure (0.008 µm/s) was almost 2 orders of magnitude slower than the speed of the EB1 comets (0.26 µm/s), and was similar to that of actin ring closure (Figure 2H, n = 4).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and Figure 2H.

claim: The speed of EB1 ring closure was similar to that of actin ring closure.
source: Notably, the speed of EB1 ring closure (0.008 µm/s) was almost 2 orders of magnitude slower than the speed of the EB1 comets (0.26 µm/s), and was similar to that of actin ring closure (Figure 2H, n = 4).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and Figure 2H.

claim: EB1 ring closure was ahead of that of actin.
source: Moreover, the specific enrichment of EB1 at the leading edge and EB1 ring closure was ahead of that of actin (Figure 2D and G, Figure 2—video 6, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and Figures 2D, 2G, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: EB1 associated with actin at the time of the formation of the ring up to its closure.
source: These results show that EB1 associated with actin at the time of the formation of the ring up to its closure.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental observations.

claim: MTs were arranged predominantly in longitudinal but haphazard bundles in the lateral epidermis.
source: We observed that MTs were arranged predominantly in longitudinal but haphazard bundles in the lateral epidermis, in marked contrast to their ordered, parallel and circumferential organisation underneath the muscle quadrants in the dorsal and ventral epidermis as well as during molting (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D), as previously described (Costa et al., 1997; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D, and citations to Costa et al., 1997 and Wang et al., 2015.

claim: EB1 comets were observed to run along MT bundles, with a preferred directionality in the A/P axis.
source: Consistent with previous reports, EB1 comets were observed to run along MT bundles, with a preferred directionality in the A/P axis as observed for MT bundles in the main epidermis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–G).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–G.

claim: After wounding, no change in the direction of EB1 comets was observed.
source: After wounding, no change in the direction of EB1 comets was observed (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and Figure 3B.

claim: MT tips were observed growing and retracting within seconds at the site of injury.
source: Detailed observations with confocal microscopy revealed MT tips growing and retracting within second at the site of injury (Figure 3C and Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and Figure 3C.

claim: At later time points, a global reorganisation of the MT network was observed as a knitting web with orthoradial MTs around the wound.
source: At later time points, a global reorganisation of the MT network was observed as a knitting web with orthoradial MTs around the wound (Figure 3D, Figure 3—videos 2 and 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and Figure 3D.

claim: After wounding, microtubules in the immediate wound periphery (R1) were perpendicular to the wound centre direction (θ ≈ 80).
source: After wounding, microtubules in the immediate wound periphery (R1) were perpendicular to the wound centre direction (θ ≈ 80).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: Such preferential orientation did not exist in controls, for example in the distant sector R3 to the wound centre nor in any sectors R1-3 before laser ablation.
source: Such preferential orientation didnot exist in controls, for example in the distant sector R3 to the wound centre nor in any sectors R1-3 before laser ablation (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and Figure 3F.

claim: MTs were not arranged radially towards the wound, but displayed an increased orthoradial orientation proximal to the wound after 10 min.
source: Thus, in concordance with the apparent random orientation of EB1 comets, these results show that MT were not arranged radially towards the wound, but displayed an increased orthoradial orientation proximal to the wound after 10 min.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental observations.

claim: MTs rapidly seed the accumulation of EB1, so facilitating the recruitment of actin, as well as knitting a webbed network around the site of injury.
source: Together, these results lead to a working model in which MTs rapidly seed the accumulation of EB1, so facilitating the recruitment of actin, as well as knitting a webbed network around the site of injury.
evidence: This is a working model based on the experimental observations.

claim: In young adult tba-2(RNAi) or tbb-2(RNAi) worms, EB1::GFP comets were no longer visible suggesting that MT dynamics had been severely compromised.
source: In young adult tba-2(RNAi) or tbb-2(RNAi) worms, EB1::GFP comets were no longer visible suggesting that MT dynamics had been severely compromised (Figure 4A and B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and Figures 4A, 4B, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The effect of tba-2(RNAi) or tbb-2(RNAi) on EB1 comets was specific to the epidermis (hyp7) since highly motile comets were still visible in the seam cells.
source: Interestingly, this effect was specific to the epidermis (hyp7) since highly motile comets were still visible in the seam cells (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: Upon wounding, EB1::GFP was not recruited to the wound site in tba-2(RNAi) or tbb-2(RNAi) worms.
source: Upon wounding, EB1::GFP was not recruited to the wound site (Figure 4A and C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and Figures 4A and 4C.

claim: Constant expression of tba-2 and tbb-2 genes is required for the normal dynamic behaviour of the non-centrosomal MTs in the epidermal syncytium.
source: This suggests that constant expression of tba-2 and tbb-2 genes is required for the normal dynamic behaviour of the non-centrosomal MTs in the epidermal syncytium, as well as for the redistribution of EB1 caused by injury.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: Constant expression of tba-2 and tbb-2 genes is required for the redistribution of EB1 caused by injury.
source: This suggests that constant expression of tba-2 and tbb-2 genes is required for the normal dynamic behaviour of the non-centrosomal MTs in the epidermal syncytium, as well as for the redistribution of EB1 caused by injury.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: Short abrogation of tbb-2 from the L4 stage altered the MT network in young adult worms, as visualised with TBB-2::GFP; it became less dense and less longitudinally structured in the lateral epidermis.
source: In resting conditions, short abrogation of tbb-2 from the L4 stage, altered the MT network in young adult worms, as visualised with TBB-2::GFP; it became less dense and less longitudinally structured in the lateral epidermis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The actin network was less dense in tbb-2(RNAi) worms.
source: The actin network was also less dense in these worms (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Upon wounding, less actin was recruited around the site of injury following tbb-2 RNAi.
source: Upon wounding, less actin was recruited around the site of injury following tbb-2 RNAi (Figure 4D and G).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and Figures 4D and 4G.

claim: Actin was recruited later in tbb-2 RNAi treated than in control worms.
source: Further, analyses of the dynamics of radial intensities across the wound revealed that as well as accumulating to lower levels, actin was recruited later in tbb-2 RNAi treated than in control worms (Figure 4E–F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and Figures 4E–F.

claim: The actin ring did not constrict as quickly in tbb-2 RNAi treated worms as in control worms, as measured by the area inside the ring after 15 min.
source: Moreover, the actin ring did not constrict as quickly as in control worms, as measured by the area inside the ring after 15 min (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and Figure 4H.

claim: Reduction of the level of actin via inactivation of act-2 did not change the overall pattern of MTs nor EB1 dynamics.
source: Notably, the relationship between MTs and actin was not reciprocal. Thus, reduction of the level of actin via inactivation of act-2 did not change the overall pattern of MTs nor EB1 dynamics (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: MT dynamics facilitate actin ring closure.
source: This suggests that MT dynamics do indeed facilitate actin ring closure.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: Knocking down tba-2 and tba-4 leads to an abrogation of the induction of the AMP gene reporter nlp-29p::GFP usually caused by Drechmeria coniospora infection.
source: We had previously demonstrated in a genome-wide RNAi screen that knocking down certain genes associated with MT function, including tba-2 and tba-4, leads to an abrogation of the induction of the AMP gene reporter nlp-29p::GFP usually caused by Drechmeria coniospora infection (Supplementary file 1-Table S1, Zugasti et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a primary finding from a previous study, supported by citation to Zugasti et al., 2016.

claim: Inactivation of tba-2 and tba-4 from the L4 stage led to a block of AMP induction after infection in the adult.
source: Using the same protocol of short inactivation from the L4 stage presented above, we confirmed that inactivation of these two tubulin α genes led to a block of AMP induction after infection in the adult (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and Figure 5A.

claim: tba-2 and tba-4 are required for AMP reporter gene induction after wounding.
source: In addition, we showed that tba-2 and tba-4 are also required for AMP reporter gene induction after wounding (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and Figure 5A.

claim: Inactivation of tubulin β genes tbb-1 and tbb-2 was associated with a block of AMP reporter gene induction upon infection.
source: In addition to tba-2 and tba-4, we found that inactivation of tubulin β genes tbb-1 and tbb-2 was also associated with a block of AMP reporter gene induction upon infection (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: The block of AMP reporter gene induction was not a consequence of reduced spore binding to the worm cuticle.
source: We found that this was not a consequence of reduced spore binding to the worm cuticle (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Inactivation of the genes that blocked the immune response altered the pattern of MTs.
source: Using the TBB-2::GFP strain, we also showed that inactivation of the genes that blocked the immune response altered the pattern of MTs, confirming the expression and functional importance of these tubulin isotypes in the adult epidermis (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Inactivation of tubulin-γ (TBG-1) expression in the adult epidermis a few hours before infection did not affect AMP reporter gene induction nor the overall MTs pattern.
source: On the other hand, inactivation of tubulin-γ (TBG-1) expression in the adult epidermis a few hours before infection did not affect AMP reporter gene induction nor the overall MTs pattern (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and Figures 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Unlike MT + ends, – ends are less dynamic in the adult epidermis and are not required for the immune response upon wounding.
source: Since tubulin-γ nucleates MTs at their minus end (Quintin et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2015), this could suggest that unlike MT + ends, – ends are less dynamic in the adult epidermis and are not required for the immune response upon wounding.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations and citations to Quintin et al., 2016 and Wang et al., 2015.

claim: MT + end dynamics appear to be required for the regulation of the transcriptional response to injury and fungal infection in the epidermis.
source: Thus, independent of their role in the maintenance of epidermal structure, and in addition to a function in mediating wound closure upon wounding, MT + end dynamics appear to be required for the regulation of the transcriptional response to injury and fungal infection in the epidermis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental observations.

claim: SNF-12 is localized in clusters at the apical surface of the hyp7 syncytium.
source: The SLC6 family member SNF-12 was a prime candidate, as we have previously shown that it is localized in clusters at the apical surface of the hyp7 syncytium (Dierking et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dierking et al., 2011.

claim: SNF-12 clusters were in the same focal plane as PIP2 and the most apical RAB-11 recycling endosomes, and apical to LAAT-1-positive lysosomes.
source: We did not detect any colocalisation, but we observed that SNF-12 clusters were in the same focal plane as PIP2 and the most apical RAB-11 recycling endosomes, and apical to LAAT-1-positive lysosomes (Figure 6A and B, Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and Figures 6A, 6B, and Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: SNF-12 is in a yet-to-be defined apical membrane compartment.
source: This indicates that SNF-12 is in a yet-to-be defined apical membrane compartment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: In the dorsal and ventral epidermis, SNF-12 was found in a banded pattern, like the highly organised circumferential cytoskeleton.
source: Interestingly, in the dorsal and ventral epidermis, SNF-12 was found in a banded pattern, like the highly organised circumferential cytoskeleton (Figure 6C, Figure 6—video 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and Figure 6C.

claim: The majority of SNF-12 clusters were static or just vibrating, with only very few moving longer straight distances, presumably along MT tracks, with a low speed of 0.017 ± 0.005 µm/s.
source: Compared to EB1 and RAB-11 (see below), the majority of SNF-12 clusters were static or just vibrating, with only very few moving longer straight distances, presumably along MT tracks, with a low speed of 0.017 ± 0.005 µm/s (Figure 6D, Figure 6—video 1, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and Figure 6D.

claim: When worms carrying the SNF-12::GFP reporter were wounded, there was a progressive recruitment of SNF-12 to the wound site.
source: When we wounded worms carrying the SNF-12::GFP reporter, we observed a progressive recruitment of SNF-12 to the wound site (Figure 6E and F, Figure 6—video 2), with the majority of the clusters around the wound moving in a directed manner at a low speed of 0.007 ± 0.004 µm/s (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and Figures 6E and 6F.

claim: When MTs were disrupted via RNAi of tba-2, SNF-12 patterning and recruitment were severely compromised.
source: When we disrupted MTs, via RNAi of tba-2, SNF-12 patterning and recruitment were severely compromised (Figure 6G–I).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and Figures 6G–I.

claim: Both EB1 and SNF-12 patterning and dynamics upon wounding were affected when the MT severing protein SPAS-1 was overexpressed in the worm epidermis.
source: Similarly, both EB1 and SNF-12 patterning and dynamics upon wounding were also affected when the MT severing protein SPAS-1 was overexpressed in the worm epidermis (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: MTs play an important role in SNF-12 localisation and dynamics and thereby in the induction of AMP gene expression.
source: Together, these results suggest that MTs play an important role in SNF-12 localisation and dynamics and thereby in the induction of AMP gene expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: The movement of SNF-12 towards the wound site was not simply a reflection of cytoplasmic flow.
source: Thus, the movement of SNF-12 towards the wound site was not simply a reflection of cytoplasmic flow.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that most vesicle markers did not show recruitment.

claim: RAB-5::GFP appeared localised in large static donut-shaped structures (0.3–0.8 µm) arranged in a reticular pattern, exchanging with smaller vesicles (0.2–0.4 µm).
source: RAB-5::GFP appeared localised in large static donut-shaped structures (0.3–0.8 µm) arranged in a reticular pattern, exchanging with smaller vesicles (0.2–0.4 µm), as described previously (Chuang et al., 2016; Figure 7A, Figure 6—video 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data, Figure 7A, and citation to Chuang et al., 2016.

claim: Upon wounding, small RAB-5 vesicles accumulated around the wound site within 10–15 min.
source: Upon wounding these small vesicles accumulated around the wound site within 10–15 min (Figure 7A, Figure 6—video 4).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and Figure 7A.

claim: RAB-11::GFP was found in extremely motile (1.31 ± 0.33 µm/s) vesicles (0.2–0.4 µm).
source: RAB-11::GFP was found in extremely motile (1.31 ± 0.33 µm/s) vesicles (0.2–0.4 µm) (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: RAB-11 vesicles moved long distances in one direction, presumably on microtubule tracks.
source: They moved long distances in one direction, presumably on microtubule tracks (Figure 6D, Figure 6—video 5).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and Figure 6D.

claim: Upon wounding, RAB-11 vesicles started to accumulate around the wound site within 10–15 min and reached a maximum density between 30 and 60 min post wounding.
source: Upon wounding they started to accumulate around the wound site within 10–15 min (Figure 7B, Figure 6—video 6) and reached a maximum density between 30 and 60 min post wounding.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and Figure 7B.

claim: Both rab-5 and rab-11 are required non-redundantly for the epidermal innate immune response to infection.
source: Notably, we previously demonstrated that both rab-5 and rab-11 are required non-redundantly for the epidermal innate immune response to infection (Dierking et al., 2011; Zugasti et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dierking et al., 2011 and Zugasti et al., 2016.

claim: The coordinated recruitment of endosomal vesicles and the uncharacterised SNF-12-associated clusters, which are both dependent upon MT reorganisation, tie together wound repair and the innate immune response.
source: The coordinated recruitment of endosomal vesicles and the uncharacterised SNF-12-associated clusters, which are both dependent upon MT reorganisation, tie together wound repair and the innate immune response.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental observations.

claim: Mutants for the p38 MAPK PMK-1 and for the SARM orthologue TIR-1 are defective for the induction of AMP gene expression after wounding.
source: Thus, although mutants for the p38 MAPK PMK-1 and for the SARM orthologue TIR-1, that acts upstream of the p38 cascade, are defective for the induction of AMP gene expression after wounding (Pujol et al., 2008a), they exhibit normal actin ring closure (Xu and Chisholm, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pujol et al., 2008a and Xu and Chisholm, 2011.

claim: Mutants for PMK-1 and TIR-1 exhibit normal actin ring closure.
source: Thus, although mutants for the p38 MAPK PMK-1 and for the SARM orthologue TIR-1, that acts upstream of the p38 cascade, are defective for the induction of AMP gene expression after wounding (Pujol et al., 2008a), they exhibit normal actin ring closure (Xu and Chisholm, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Xu and Chisholm, 2011.

claim: Cytoskeleton components can play a role in regulating AMP production.
source: If innate immune signal transduction pathway components are not required for wound repair, our results suggest, on the other hand, that cytoskeleton components can play a role in regulating AMP production.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: Several tubulin genes are required for AMP expression upon infection and wounding, potentially through their effect on the localization and dynamics of innate immune signalling proteins including SNF-12.
source: Indeed, several tubulin genes are required for AMP expression upon infection and wounding, potentially through their effect on the localization and dynamics of innate immune signalling proteins including SNF-12.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: Overexpression in the epidermis of the MT severing protein Spastin caused a similar effect on SNF-12 dynamics as knocking down tubulin expression, supporting a role for MTs in positioning SNF-12-containing vesicles.
source: The fact that overexpression in the epidermis of the MT severing protein Spastin caused a similar effect on SNF-12 dynamics as knocking down tubulin expression, supports a role for MTs in positioning SNF-12-containing vesicles.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: Spatial regulation of signalling may contribute to restricting defence gene activation to the immediate vicinity of a wound or site of infection within the major epidermal syncytium.
source: We speculate that this spatial regulation of signalling may contribute to restricting defence gene activation to the immediate vicinity of a wound or site of infection within the major epidermal syncytium.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental observations.

claim: Loss of dapk-1 function causes defects in the epidermis that result from the hyperstabilisation of MTs.
source: Interestingly, dapk-1 mutants have defects in the epidermis that were shown to result from the hyperstabilisation of MTs.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from prior work.

claim: DAPK-1 inhibits the function of PTRN-1, a MT - end binding protein, which acts as a MT nucleator and promotes MT stabilization.
source: DAPK-1 inhibits the function of PTRN-1, a MT - end binding protein, which acts as a MT nucleator and promotes MT stabilization.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from prior work.

claim: Loss of ptrn-1 function suppresses the epidermal defects seen in dapk-1 mutants as well as their constitutive AMP gene expression and accelerated wound closure.
source: Loss of ptrn-1 function suppresses the epidermal defects seen in dapk-1 mutants as well as their constitutive AMP gene expression and accelerated wound closure.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from prior work.

claim: Loss of dapk-1 function is associated with an increase in EB1 comets.
source: Loss of dapk-1 function is associated with an increase in EB1 comets.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from prior work.

claim: The increase in EB1 comets in dapk-1 mutants is suppressed in a dapk-1;ptrn-1 double mutant.
source: This too is suppressed in a dapk-1;ptrn-1 double mutant (Chuang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chuang et al., 2016.

claim: The accelerated wound healing seen in dapk-1 mutant worms may be due to an increased recruitment of EB1 protein thus speeding up MT-dependent actin ring closure.
source: Taken together with our results, this suggests that the accelerated wound healing seen in dapk-1 mutant worms may be due to an increased recruitment of EB1 protein thus speeding up MT-dependent actin ring closure.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations and prior work.
